articles.title: I couldn't say in one sentence what to tell users when we used AI. So I built a drafter.
articles.excerpt: We shipped a feature that used a model to summarize support tickets. Quietly. And then a reviewer asked the only question that mattered: when a user reads the output, are we telling them it was genera…
articles.body: We shipped a feature that used a model to summarize support tickets. Quietly. And then a reviewer asked the only question that mattered: when a user reads the output, are we telling them it was generated by AI? I didn't have an answer, and the EU AI Act expects one. Articles 49 and 50 of the Act are about exactly this — telling people when AI is involved, whether that's a general-purpose model's capabilities or AI-generated content a user might mistake for human-made. The obligation is concrete wording, aimed at the user, at the point of interaction. I kept getting it wrong because "disclose that AI was used" is a sentence, not a disclosure.

articles.title: dlt's Auto-Schema Pipeline: How Python Data Loaders Infer Structure Without Predefined Models
articles.excerpt: Agent-driven data pipelines break when upstream APIs change field types, add nested objects, or return inconsistent structures. Traditional ETL requires manual schema definitions, which means every AP…
articles.body: Agent-driven data pipelines break when upstream APIs change field types, add nested objects, or return inconsistent structures. Traditional ETL requires manual schema definitions, which means every API evolution triggers a pull request, a migration script, and downtime. dlt is an open-source Python library that infers schemas on the fly, writes to SQL stores, vector databases, DuckDB, and data lakes, and handles schema drift without predefined models. The library shipped with 222 points on Show HN and 54 comments. It targets the exact problem agents face: ingesting messy, unstructured data from scrapers, APIs, and webhooks without brittle DDL.

Today, Johnson serves as NASA’s Center of Excellence for Human Spaceflight, and its workforce is helping to usher in a Golden Age of innovation and discovery. articles.title: Viltrox AF 35mm f/1.8 II EVO FE (APO) lens review — how good is this budget lens for astrophotography?
articles.excerpt: The Viltrox AF 35mm f/1.8 II FE (APO) is an inexpensive prime that works well for astrophotography thanks to its focal length and maximum aperture.
articles.body: Key specs Type: Full-frame prime lens Focal length: 35 mm Maximum aperture: f/1.8 Lens mount: Sony FE & Nikon Z Weight: 12.52 oz / 355 g Dimensions: 3.33 x 4.37 in / 69 x 76 mm Filter thread: 58 mm Release date: April 2026 Budget primes can be, surprisingly, excellent choices for photographers shooting all subjects. It’s all too easy to get carried away with the best specs, such as a large maximum aperture and impressive optical design often seen in more expensive options. But affordable lenses like the Viltrox AF 35mm f/1.8 II FE (APO) have the potential to impress and delight in equal measure. The 35mm f/1.8 is a compact and lightweight lens offering a reasonably fast maximum aperture, making it a prime candidate for astrophotography.

articles.title: NASA’s CHAPEA Crew “Returns” to Earth
articles.excerpt: The four-member Crew Health and Performance Exploration Analog (CHAPEA) crew poses outside for the first time in more than a year following the end of their simulated Mars journey on Oct. 31, 2026. Cr…
articles.body: NASA/James Blair The four-member Crew Health and Performance Exploration Analog (CHAPEA) crew poses outside for the first time in more than a year following the end of their simulated Mars journey on Oct. 31, 2026. Crew members Matthew Montgomery (left), James Spicer (middle left), Ross Elder (middle right), and Ellen Ellis (right) spent more than a year testing systems, maintaining crops, managing limited resources and communication delays, conducting extravehicular activities and more in efforts to help NASA better understand how crews adapt to long-duration stays. Insights from their experiences will help NASA design its future Moon Base and plan for missions on Mars. Image credit: NASA/James Blair
